report:
## Conclusion

The evidence supports the claim, with some nuance: **higher olive oil consumption, particularly as part of a Mediterranean-style diet, is associated with a reduced risk of stroke**, though the strength of this effect varies by study design and dose.

The strongest evidence comes from the randomized **PREDIMED trial**, which found that a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil reduced cardiovascular events, "particularly stroke," compared to a lower-fat control diet (ahajournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1161/hypertensionaha.113.03353). This is a randomized controlled trial, giving it high causal weight.

Observational meta-analyses of case-control, cohort, and intervention studies (Martínez-González et al.) found a dose-response relationship, with each 25g/day increment of olive oil intake associated with a 24% lower relative risk of stroke (researchgate.net/publication/261954820). Large U.S. cohorts (Nurses' Health Study and Health Professionals Follow-Up Study) similarly link greater olive oil intake to lower cardiovascular disease risk broadly, including stroke, and lower cardiovascular mortality (jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.10.041).

However, some caveats exist: a 2020 meta-analysis reportedly found no significant association between olive oil and stroke specifically (per Healthline summary), and effects may be partly confounded by other Mediterranean diet components (vegetables, fruits, whole grains) that typically accompany higher olive oil intake, as noted in some cohort analyses.

**Bottom line:** The overall body of evidence—especially the randomized PREDIMED trial—supports that olive oil, especially extra-virgin, likely reduces stroke risk, most robustly when consumed as part of an overall healthy dietary pattern rather than in isolation.
